title: Three Days in the Mountains
paragraphs: Last summer my family spent three days in a village in the mountains. There was one road, one shop and no phone signal.
The first day I was bored. I had brought two books and finished one by lunchtime. In the afternoon I walked to the end of the road and back.
By the third day I had stopped counting the hours. I was not bored any more; I was simply busy with small things.
On the way home the signal came back on my phone. I looked at it, and then I put it away for another hour.
Three days was enough. A fourth would have been too many.

title: What a Holiday Is For
paragraphs: People describe holidays as a break from work. But most holidays are more tiring than the working week.
We get up early to catch a train, walk for eight hours, take photographs and eat too much. We come home and need a holiday.
The trouble is that a described holiday is not the same as a restful one. They are two different products.
So the useful question before a trip is not where to go, but which of the two you need this time.
The best holidays I remember were cheap ones. Nobody was in a hurry, and each day had only one plan in it.

title: The Holiday I Learned From
paragraphs: When I was eleven, my parents let me plan a two-day trip by myself. It was a small trip, to a town two hours away.
I made three mistakes. I booked a hotel far from the station. I planned four places for one afternoon. I did not check that the museum closed on Mondays.
On the train home my father asked what I would change. I said everything, and he laughed.
Since then I have planned every family trip. I am much better at it, and I still check the opening days first.
That mistake cost us one afternoon. The lesson has saved us about ten.

title: A Postcard Home
paragraphs: Dear Grandma,
We are in a small town by the sea. The hotel is old and the lift does not work, but our room looks onto the water.
Every morning fishermen bring their boats in at about six. I have watched them three times and I still do not understand how the nets work.
The food is very simple: rice, fish, and a soup with a name I cannot pronounce. I have eaten it four days in a row.
We come home on Friday. I will bring you the dried fish you asked for, and a photograph of the boats.
Love, Mei
P.S. The train leaves at seven. Do not be late again.

title: Talking About a Trip
paragraphs: Ben: How was your trip to Xi'an?
Amy: Good, but crowded. The museum was fully booked for three days.
Ben: Did you see the terracotta soldiers? Amy: Yes, we got tickets for the last morning.
Ben: Was it worth it? Amy: It was. I stood in front of them for twenty minutes and said nothing.
Ben: And the food? Amy: Better than the soldiers, honestly. I had noodles four times.
Ben: Would you go again? Amy: In winter, yes. Not in July.
Ben: Noted. Amy: And book the museum a week early. I am serious.
Ben: I will book it tonight. Amy: And set an alarm this time.

title: The Photograph I Did Not Take
paragraphs: There is a photograph I did not take, and I still think about it.
It was in a village in Yunnan. An old woman was sitting on a low wall, mending a basket. Behind her the sun was going down over the fields.
I had my camera in my hand. I raised it, and then I stopped, because she had looked up and seen me.
I asked if I could take a picture. She shook her head and smiled, and went back to the basket.
I have hundreds of photographs from that trip. I remember that one minute better than all of them.
That minute is the clearest thing I brought home.

title: Why We Bring Back Souvenirs
paragraphs: Every tourist shop sells the same three things: a magnet, a key ring and a small model of a famous building.
Nobody needs these objects. They are bought because a holiday feels incomplete without something to carry home.
This is why the ugliest objects are often kept longest. Their value has nothing to do with how they look.
I have a stone from a beach in Fujian. It is a grey stone. It has been on my desk for nine years.
It cost nothing and does nothing. But when I hold it I am on that beach again, with wet shoes and a bag of hot bread.

title: Who Does the Most
paragraphs: In most families, one person does more housework than everybody else, and it is usually not the person who thinks so.
Studies that ask family members to estimate their share find a consistent pattern: almost everyone overestimates their own contribution.
So the argument about housework is rarely about laziness. It is about visibility.
The families that argue least are usually the ones with a written list. A list makes invisible work visible, and then the argument is about facts.
A list works better when everyone writes it than when one person hands it out.

title: The Kitchen Light
paragraphs: In my house, the kitchen light is always on. My mother leaves it on when she goes to bed, in case somebody comes home late.
For years I thought this was carelessness. I turned it off every night and she turned it back on.
Then I went to stay with a friend for a week. His house was dark at midnight, and I found it strange and a little cold.
When I came back, I left the light on myself. Nobody asked me why.
A house is not made of walls. It is made of these small arrangements that only make sense to the people inside.

title: Moving House
paragraphs: We moved when I was twelve. It was four streets away, which sounds small and is not.
The new flat was bigger and brighter. My room had a window facing east, so I woke up early for the first month.
What fixed it was a broken chair. My father repaired it in the new living room, with the same tools and the same complaining.
After that the flat was ours. Home, it turns out, is not the building. It is the set of habits you bring into it.
Two months later I stopped hearing the road, and my mother stopped apologising for the kitchen. That is when a place becomes yours.

title: Rules at Home
paragraphs: Mum: We need to talk about the weekends.
Tom: What about them? Mum: You come home at eleven and nobody knows where you are.
Tom: I am with friends. Mum: I know. I still want a message at nine.
Tom: That is every weekend? Mum: Every weekend. One message, one line. Then I sleep.
Tom: All right. And if I forget? Mum: Then I call you, and you will not like the conversation.
Tom: What if my phone is dead? Mum: Then borrow one. There is always somebody with a phone.

title: My Grandparents' Village House
paragraphs: My grandparents' house has one room that nobody uses. It is kept exactly as it was when my great-grandmother lived there.
There is a wooden bed, a table, a mirror and a photograph. Nothing has been moved for thirty years.
My grandmother cleans it once a month. She does not sit in it. She opens the window, dusts the table, and closes the door.
I asked her once why she keeps it. She said, because it is still her room.
I did not understand this when I was ten. Now I think it is the most sensible thing in the house.

title: Why Small Flats Feel Bigger
paragraphs: A small flat can feel larger than a big one, and the reason is usually not the area.
The first factor is sight lines. If you can see from the door to the window without a wall in the way, the space reads as one room.
The third is light. A room with one small window feels smaller than the same room with a wide one, because the eye needs an exit.
So the design question is not how many square metres you have. It is how many places your eye can go.
A mirror at the end of a corridor adds three metres that do not exist. So does a window you can see from the door.

title: Two Brothers
paragraphs: My brother and I are two years apart and share a room, a school and most of our friends.
People assume we are similar. We are not. He decides in a minute and regrets it for a week. I decide in a week and never regret it.
The arrangement works because we divided the room without discussing it. He has the window side, I have the wall side.
We also divided the arguments. He is allowed to be angry first. I am allowed to be right later.
This is not a rule anybody wrote down. It took about three years and one broken lamp.

title: Why Difference Is Useful
paragraphs: Groups of similar people are comfortable and weak. This is not an opinion; it is a pattern found in many studies of decision making.
When everyone has the same background, they share the same blind spots. Nobody notices the missing question, because nobody thinks to ask it.
The condition is that the difference must be allowed to speak. A group with one quiet outsider is still a group of similar people.
So the value is not diversity itself. It is disagreement that is safe to express.
A group where nobody dares to disagree is quiet, not peaceful.

title: The New Student
paragraphs: A new student joined our class in October. She had moved from another province and spoke with a different accent.
For two weeks she sat alone at lunch. Not because anybody was unkind, but because nobody had a reason to sit with her.
She was very good at it. She had done the same project at her old school and knew which design would hold the most weight.
By Friday she had four people asking her questions. A project did what two weeks of good intentions could not.
She was not shy. She had simply been given nothing to do for two weeks.

title: Comparing Two Schools
paragraphs: I changed schools in Grade Eight, so I can compare two systems from the inside.
The first school had fifty students in a class and one teacher. The second has thirty-eight and two, for some subjects.
Neither is simply better. The first made me fast and accurate. The second made me better at planning and speaking.
What I noticed most is that both schools believed they were normal. That is what a system does: it makes itself invisible.
At my school one bell rings for everyone at once and nobody finds it strange. Neither system is natural; both are simply old.

title: Agreeing to Disagree
paragraphs: Amy: I think school should start at nine.
Ben: Then it would end at five. I would rather finish at four.
Amy: We could shorten the lunch break. Ben: Lunch is the only hour I am awake.
Amy: That is not true. Ben: It is half true. Look, we agree on the problem.
Amy: Do we? Ben: Yes. Neither of us wants to get up at six thirty.
Amy: All right. Then let us write that down and argue about the solution later.
Ben: Write it down, then. Amy: Problem: nobody wants to get up at six thirty.
Ben: Good. Now we can argue about something real.

title: The Same Rain
paragraphs: Two people can stand in the same rain and have opposite days.
One is a farmer whose field has been dry for a month. The other is a bride whose wedding is outdoors.
Nothing about the rain is different. What differs is the plan it interrupts.
This is why arguments about facts often fail. People are not usually disagreeing about the fact; they are disagreeing about whether the fact is good.
So before asking who is right, it helps to ask what each person needed the day to be.
The rain was the same. The afternoon was not, and both of us were telling the truth.

title: The Tree That Shares
paragraphs: In a forest, trees are connected underground by a network of fungus. The fungus attaches to the roots of many trees at once.
Water and minerals travel through this network. So does sugar, in small amounts, from trees that have more to trees that have less.
Scientists disagree about how much this matters. Some say it is a small effect. Others say it changes how we should think about a forest.
Either way, the old picture of trees as separate individuals is wrong. A forest is a system, not a collection.

title: Why Flowers Have Colours
paragraphs: A flower's colour is advertising. It is not for us; it is for insects and birds.
Red flowers are often visited by birds, because birds see red well. Yellow and blue flowers attract bees.
Some flowers have patterns invisible to humans but visible to insects, because insects see ultraviolet light.
Scent does the same job at night, when colour is useless. That is why white flowers often smell strongest.
So a flower is a message with a target audience. Change the audience, and the message changes.
Colour costs the plant energy, so it only pays when there is a customer.

title: The Ant and the Acacia
paragraphs: In Central America there is a tree called the acacia, and an ant that lives only on that tree.
The tree provides hollow thorns for the ants to live in, and small sweet packets on its leaves for them to eat.
Experiments show that acacias without ants grow more slowly and are eaten more often.
This kind of arrangement is called mutualism. Both sides give something and both sides receive something. Neither could easily live alone.
The acacia also makes a chemical that tastes bad once the ants are gone. The tree is not helpless; it is slow.

title: Should We Bring Back Lost Species?
paragraphs: Scientists can now edit the genes of living animals. Some have suggested using this to bring back extinct species.
The argument for it is that we caused the extinctions, so we should repair them.
A mammoth without a steppe is a zoo animal with an interesting history.
There is also a practical question. Money spent on bringing back one species could protect a hundred that are still here. That trade is the real decision.
And there is a third question that nobody likes. If we bring a species back, where does it live? The place it came from is a road or a farm now.

title: The Plant on My Desk
paragraphs: There is a plant on my desk that I have kept alive for three years, which surprises everybody including me.
It is a small succulent. I water it once every two weeks, and in summer I forget and it survives anyway.
A plant does not need your attention. It needs light and a little water, and then it needs you to leave it alone.
I have killed seven plants learning this. The eighth one is doing very well.
What I learned is that most plants do not die of neglect. They die of kindness. Watered twice a week and moved to a bigger pot, mine drowned in soil that never dried.

title: Why Pandas Are Difficult
paragraphs: Pandas are famous, protected and expensive, and the reason is an unusual diet.
A panda's digestive system is that of a carnivore. It cannot process bamboo efficiently.
So it must eat a lot: ten to fifteen kilos a day, for ten to twelve hours.
This is why pandas cannot travel far, cannot hibernate, and cannot survive in a small reserve. They must always be near a large bamboo supply.
Protecting a panda therefore means protecting a forest, not an animal. This is true of most endangered species, which is why the popular image is misleading.

title: The First Dish I Cooked
paragraphs: The first dish I cooked alone was tomato and egg. I was eleven and my mother was ill.
I had watched her make it a hundred times, so I was confident. I put the oil in, then the egg, and the pan caught fire slightly.
I turned off the gas and put a lid on it, which is what she always did. The fire went out.
The dish was not good. The egg was dry and the tomato was raw. My mother ate all of it.
I can make it properly now. It took about ten attempts and one serious conversation about heat.
The serious conversation was about one thing: the pan must be hot before the egg goes in.

title: Why Recipes Use Exact Amounts
paragraphs: A recipe says two hundred grams of flour and one teaspoon of salt. A grandmother says a bowl and a pinch.
Both work, and the difference is feedback. A grandmother cooks the same dish every week and adjusts by eye.
A recipe is written for someone who cannot adjust, so it removes the decisions.
This is why baking recipes are exact and stir-fry recipes are vague. Baking is chemistry: the ratio decides the result.
A stir-fry can be corrected halfway through. A cake cannot. Exactness appears where correction is impossible.

title: The Soup That Takes Four Hours
paragraphs: My uncle makes a soup that takes four hours. He starts at nine in the morning for a lunch at one.
The first hour is only bones and water, boiling hard, then poured away. He says this is the most important hour.
The next three hours are low heat. The pot barely moves. He adds ginger, then nothing else.
At the end there is salt, added in three small amounts, tasting in between.
I once asked why he does not use a pressure cooker. He said it takes twenty minutes and tastes like twenty minutes. I did not argue.

title: Food and Memory
paragraphs: Food is one of the strongest memory triggers, and the reason is partly chemical.
Smell goes directly to the part of the brain that handles memory and emotion, bypassing the usual relay station.
But there is a social layer too. The dishes we remember are the ones somebody made for us, repeatedly, at a particular time of life.
So a recipe is never only a recipe. It carries the person who cooked it, which is why families argue about the correct way to make things that taste identical.
Two sisters can cook from the same recipe and each will say the other has it wrong.

title: Cooking as a Life Skill
paragraphs: Schools teach algebra for six years and cooking for one term, if at all. This is a strange set of priorities.
Cooking is not a hobby. It is the skill you use every day for the rest of your life, and the one that most directly affects your health.
And it teaches failure. A dish that goes wrong is visible, immediate and not serious. That is a good way to learn that mistakes are survivable.
So one term is not enough, and it should not be optional.
Someone who can cook four dishes can feed himself for life. Someone who cannot depends on other people's moods.

title: The Plan That Worked
paragraphs: In September I made a plan to improve my English. It had one line: twenty minutes a day, before dinner.
No app, no list of grammar points, no weekly test. One line and a fixed time.
I missed four days in the first month and eleven in the second. I did not restart the count or punish myself.
By January I had read two short novels in English. Not well, but without stopping.
The plan worked because it was small enough to survive a bad day. Every plan I made before this one failed for the opposite reason.

title: Why Plans Fail
paragraphs: Most plans fail in the second week, and the reason is almost never laziness.
The first cause is size. A plan that needs ninety minutes cannot survive a Monday.
The second is vagueness. Study more is not a plan. Study page forty to forty-five at eight o'clock is.
The third is all-or-nothing thinking. One missed day becomes a failed plan, and a failed plan becomes permission to stop.
So a good plan has three features: it is small, it is specific, and it assumes you will miss days. The last one is the one people forget.

title: Two Lists
paragraphs: There are two kinds of list, and mixing them up causes most of the stress in a school week.
The first is a task list: things to do, in no particular order. It has no times and no end.
The second is a schedule: things to do at particular times. It is fixed and it can be full.
A task list is for choosing. A schedule is for doing. Confusing them means either a list you never start or a day with no room.
The method that works is simple: write the tasks, pick three, then put those three into times. Three, not ten.

title: What I Want in Five Years

So my picture has a small kitchen, one shelf of books, a window facing east, and work that lets me be home by seven.

title: The Timetable on the Wall

She drew it herself: seven columns for the days, and rows for the hours from seven in the evening to eleven.

I copied the idea. It is the only study method I have ever kept for more than a month.

title: The City in 2050
paragraphs: Predictions about cities usually fall into three groups: transport, energy and food.
Transport is the easiest to predict. Most cars in 2050 will probably be electric, and many will be shared rather than owned.
Energy is harder. Solar and wind will be cheaper, but storing electricity is still the unsolved problem.
Food is the most uncertain. Vertical farming works for vegetables and costs too much for grain.
So the honest forecast is uneven. Some parts of daily life will change completely and others will look almost the same.

title: The Prediction That Was Wrong
paragraphs: In the 1960s, many experts predicted that by the year 2000 nobody would work more than twenty hours a week.
Machines would do the labour. People would have a problem: too much free time.
The forecast was half right. Machines did take over much of the work.
But the working week did not shrink. The saved time went into new tasks that nobody had imagined, and into being available all the time.
The lesson is not that prediction is useless. It is that prediction usually gets the technology right and the human arrangement wrong.

title: Learning to Drive in 2040

So I will learn to drive anyway. Not because I will need to, but because I want to understand the thing that moves me.

title: The Job That Does Not Exist Yet
paragraphs: Half the jobs people do today did not exist fifty years ago. This is not an unusual situation; it is the normal one.
New jobs usually appear where two old things meet. A data analyst is a statistician who works with computers.
A user experience designer is a psychologist who works with software. A drone pilot is a photographer who works with aircraft.
So predicting future jobs is less useful than noticing which two fields are beginning to overlap.
The skill that survives is not a specific tool. It is the ability to learn the next tool.

title: Why We Like Disaster Films
paragraphs: Disaster films are popular, and the reason is not that people enjoy suffering.
In a disaster film the world becomes simple. There is one problem, it is visible, and everybody agrees what to do about it.
Real problems are not like that. They are slow, disputed, and caused by things we are not willing to change.
So the film offers a relief that real life does not: a clear enemy and a clear ending.
This is also why the films are less popular when real disasters are in the news. Fiction needs distance to be entertaining.

title: The Message I Should Not Have Sent
paragraphs: Last year I sent a message to a friend at eleven at night. It was three sentences and it was angry.
I wrote it in two minutes and read it once. I did not read it aloud, which is the mistake.
In the morning she had replied with one line: I do not understand what you are angry about.
I read my message again. She was right. It was angry about something I had not named.
We talked for an hour that afternoon. Now I have a rule: no message about feelings after ten o'clock.
The rule has saved me twice. Both times I was right, and the message would still have made it worse.

title: Why Text Messages Cause Trouble
paragraphs: Text removes three things that speech depends on: tone, face and timing.
Without tone, a short sentence reads as cold. Without a face, irony looks like seriousness. Without timing, a pause becomes a silence of hours.
This is why people add emojis. They are not decoration; they are a substitute for tone.
So the rule is simple. Anything with feeling in it should be said, not typed. If it must be typed, add the tone in words.
Three lines of text have no face, no pause, and no way to take a word back. A voice can soften a sentence while it is being said. A screen cannot.

title: Listening Is Not Waiting

It also requires silence. If you answer within one second, you were not listening; you were preparing.
This is a skill you can practise, and the practice is uncomfortable, because it means being quiet while somebody finishes a sentence you have already understood.

title: Why Some People Never Ask
paragraphs: In every class there are students who never ask a question, and it is rarely because they understand everything.
The usual reason is the fear of looking foolish in front of thirty people. One bad experience in Grade Five can last for years.
What works is making the question ordinary: asking the class a question nobody can answer, admitting when the teacher does not know, and answering a weak question as carefully as a good one.
The barrier is not confidence. It is the calculation of risk, and the risk has to be lowered by somebody else.

title: The Hour I Do Nothing
paragraphs: Every day at about four, I stop working for an hour. I do not read, I do not watch anything, and I do not sleep.
At first this was uncomfortable. An empty hour feels like a waste, and I kept reaching for my phone.
The strange result is that I get more done afterwards. The hour is not lost; it is borrowed, and it comes back with interest.
My friends think this is a waste of time. I have stopped explaining it. The hour works whether or not anybody agrees.
An hour a day is fifteen days a year. I have never regretted one of them.

title: Why Free Time Is Not Free
paragraphs: Free time is the only kind of time that comes with instructions.
We are told to use it well: learn a language, take up a sport, read the classics. A weekend spent doing nothing now needs an excuse.
The trouble is that rest, by definition, cannot be productive. If it is producing something, it is work with better lighting.
So the useful question is not what to do with your free time. It is whether you can spend an hour without answering that question.
Most people cannot. That is why the first twenty minutes feel wrong, and why the hour is worth keeping.

title: Hobbies That Go Nowhere
paragraphs: My uncle collects bus timetables. Not buses, not tickets. The printed timetables that used to hang at stops.

He does not show them to anybody. They are in a box under his bed, and twice a year he takes them out and looks at them.
I asked him why. He said that a timetable is a promise: this bus will come at this time, whether or not you are there.
There is no money in this hobby and no use. He is the happiest person I know.

title: A Weekend Without a Screen
paragraphs: Last month my family agreed to spend one weekend without phones, tablets or television. It was my sister's idea, and we all said yes too quickly.

title: The Value of Boredom
paragraphs: Boredom has a bad reputation, and it is undeserved.

title: Sleep Debt
paragraphs: Sleep debt is the difference between the sleep you need and the sleep you get. It accumulates.
Two hours short every night for a week is fourteen hours of debt. One long Saturday cannot repay it.
The repair is not a single long sleep. It is a return to a regular schedule, with the same bedtime every night.
This is why sleeping until noon on Sunday often makes Monday worse. It moves the body clock later, and Monday arrives an hour too early.
The debt is real and it cannot be paid in one long night. It is paid back half an hour at a time.

title: What Stress Does to the Body
paragraphs: Stress is not only a feeling. It is a set of physical changes, and they are useful in short bursts.
The heart beats faster, breathing quickens, muscles tense, and sugar is released into the blood. The body is preparing to act.
Long-term stress affects sleep, digestion and the immune system. People under it catch more colds and heal more slowly.
So the problem is not stress itself. It is stress that never gets switched off. Exercise, sleep and talking to somebody all help switch it off.
The body has one switch, and it is not in the mind.

title: Why Teenagers Argue More

title: The Reef

A bleached reef is not dead, but it is starving. If the temperature drops soon, it can recover. If not, it dies.

The seeds wait years for one good rain. Some will not open at all. They are waiting for the next one.

title: Why We Need Wild Places

This is uncomfortable and it is useful. It is the experience of being one species among many, in a place that was not built for you.
So wild places are not only for recreation. They correct a mistaken idea about our own importance.

title: The Earthquake Warning

title: Why Some Places Flood More

title: Silence Means Different Things
paragraphs: In some cultures silence after a question means the person is thinking. In others it means disagreement, or respect.
This is one of the most common sources of misunderstanding in international meetings.
A visitor from a culture where silence is uncomfortable will fill the pause with more talking, which can be read as pressure.
A visitor from a culture where silence is respectful will wait, which can be read as not understanding.
The fix is not to learn every rule. It is to say out loud what the pause means: take your time, I am listening.

title: Food Rules
paragraphs: Every culture has food rules, and they are rarely about nutrition.
Some rules concern what can be eaten together. Some concern the order of dishes. Some concern who eats first.
In most of them, the rule marks a boundary: this is us, and that is not us.
This is why food travels badly. A dish can be copied exactly and still feel wrong, because the rules around it were left behind.
So when a food becomes international, it usually changes. That is not a loss. It is what happens when a thing moves.
The dumpling travelled and became a gyoza. Both are good.

title: Staying With a Family
paragraphs: I stayed with a family in another country for three weeks as part of a school exchange.
The first days were a series of small confusions. When to shower. Whether to finish everything on the plate. Whether to help in the kitchen.
I got the plate wrong. I left food, thinking it was polite, and my host mother looked worried that I did not like it.
After that I finished everything, and she was pleased, and I was too full for a week.
By the third week I had stopped thinking about the rules. That is when the stay became interesting.

title: Learning a Language Abroad
paragraphs: People say the fastest way to learn a language is to live where it is spoken. This is only half true.
Living abroad gives you hours of input, which is necessary and hard to get otherwise.
The learners who improve fastest are the ones who accept being boring. They say the same simple sentences a hundred times, and they do not wait until they can say something clever.
So the condition is not the country. It is a willingness to sound like a child for a few months.
The first month is the hardest. You will say simple things well and clever things badly, and that order cannot be changed.

title: Two Ways to Say No
paragraphs: Amy: Did you ask him? Ben: I did. He said it might be difficult.
Amy: So he said no. Ben: He did not say no. He said it might be difficult.
Amy: In his office, that means no. Ben: How do you know?
Amy: Because he also said he would try. People who will actually do it give you a date.
Ben: So I should ask someone else? Amy: Ask him once more with a date. If he does not give one, ask someone else.
Ben: All right. I will ask for a date. Amy: And if he says next week, that is a yes.
Ben: If he says soon, that is a no. Amy: You are learning.

title: The Book I Read Too Early
paragraphs: I read a famous novel when I was eleven because it was on a list. I understood the words and nothing else.
I did not finish it. I told people it was boring, which was not true; it was simply beyond me.
At fifteen I tried again, for a class. This time I could not put it down, and I read it in four days.
The book had not changed. I had. There were things in it that required having been fourteen to notice.
So now I keep a shelf of books I failed at. It is a short shelf, and it gets shorter every year.

title: Why Reading Fiction Changes You
paragraphs: Reading fiction is often defended as a way to learn about other lives. That is true, but it is not the main effect.
The stronger effect is practice in understanding people who are not present. A novel gives you access to a mind from the inside.
Several studies find that readers of literary fiction score higher on tests of empathy. The effect is small and debated, but it is consistent.
So fiction is not entertainment with a lesson attached. The practice is the point.
On paper you have lived through a war and a funeral before you are sixteen.

title: How to Read a Difficult Book
paragraphs: Most people give up on a difficult book in the first thirty pages, and the reason is a wrong expectation.
The expectation is that reading should feel smooth. For a difficult book, it will not, and that is not a sign of failure.
Second, read the first chapter twice. The beginning is where the writer establishes a voice you are not used to.
Third, keep a piece of paper for names. Most confusion in difficult books is not about ideas; it is about who is speaking.
Fourth, reread the last page before starting the next chapter. Difficult books are built on what you have just read.

title: The Library at the End of the Road
paragraphs: There is a small library at the end of our road. It has two rooms and about six thousand books.
It is open four days a week, run by two retired teachers and a rota of volunteers.
The volunteers collected four hundred signatures in a week. Most of them were from people who had not borrowed a book in a year.
The library stayed open. I asked one of the teachers why she thought it worked, and she said: because people could walk there.
People could walk there. That sounds like nothing and it decided everything. A library three bus stops away is a library most children never enter.

title: Reading on a Screen
paragraphs: People say screens are killing reading. The evidence is more complicated.
Studies find that readers remember less from a screen than from paper, especially for long texts with a sequence of events.
The likely reason is navigation. On paper you remember where something was: top of a left-hand page. A screen has no fixed place.
This does not mean screens are bad for reading. It means they are bad for a particular kind of reading.
So a practical rule: short texts, news, messages on a screen. Anything you need to hold in your head, on paper.

title: The Book My Father Gave Me
paragraphs: When I turned thirteen, my father gave me a book he had read at the same age. It was old and the cover was loose.
He did not say why. He said, read it when you want to, and put it on my desk.
I left it there for four months. Then one rainy Sunday I opened it.
There were pencil marks in the margins, in handwriting that was not his. He had bought it second-hand, forty years earlier.
I never asked about the marks. I have added some of my own, and the book is now unreadable to anybody else, which seems right.

title: The Sunday Class
paragraphs: Every Sunday morning, about fifteen children come to a room above a shop to learn English.
The teachers are four high school students, including me. Nobody is paid.
The first month was chaos. We had prepared lessons and the children did not want them.
So we changed the approach: we played games and taught the words inside the games. Attendance doubled.
I have learned more about teaching in six months than in six years of being taught. The main lesson is that attention cannot be demanded, only earned.

title: Small Help and Big Help
paragraphs: People want their help to matter, and mattering usually means being large. This is a mistake.
A large project requires money, organisation and time. Most people have none of these in the quantity required.
A small action requires an hour. There are many hours in a week.
The arithmetic favours the small action: one hour a week for a year is fifty hours, which is more than most people give in a lifetime of good intentions.
So the question is not what would solve the problem. It is what you will still be doing in six months.

title: The Volunteer Who Quit
paragraphs: My friend volunteered at an animal shelter for two months and then stopped.
She felt guilty about it for a long time. She had told people she would stay for a year.
The shelter was not sorry to lose her. They said most volunteers leave after six weeks, and the ones who stay are the ones who like cleaning.
This is worth knowing before promising anything. The useful question is not whether you care, but whether you can do the boring part.
The boring part is showing up on a wet Saturday, for the fourth time, when nobody thanks you.

title: Should Volunteering Be Required?
paragraphs: Some schools require students to complete a fixed number of volunteer hours. Many students resent it.
The case for it is that most people never start. A requirement creates the first experience, and some of those become voluntary.
Both are true, which suggests the design matters more than the principle.
A requirement works if the placement is meaningful and the hours are few. It fails if students are sent to move chairs for forty hours to fill a form.
Forty hours of moving chairs teaches students that service is a form to be filled. Four hours of real work teaches something else.

title: The Old Man and the Bus Stop
paragraphs: An old man near our building used to complain about the bus stop. The shelter leaked, so people stood in the rain.
He complained for two years. Then he stopped complaining and started writing letters.
He wrote to the bus company, the district office and the local newspaper. He kept copies in a folder.
After eleven months, a new shelter was built. He was not invited to anything and there was no ceremony.
I asked him if he was proud. He said he was tired, and then he said: now I have to find something else to do.

title: Asking Before Helping
paragraphs: Volunteer: We are giving out blankets tonight. Do you need one?
Man: No. But the man in the blue tent does. He will not ask.
Volunteer: Why not? Man: Because he has been here three years and he has his pride.
Volunteer: How should I approach him? Man: Do not offer. Ask him if he knows anyone who needs one.
Volunteer: Then he can take it without asking. Man: Now you understand.
Volunteer: And if he refuses? Man: Then he refuses. You have still treated him like a person.
Volunteer: How long have you been doing this? Man: Six winters. The blankets change. The pride does not.

title: What I Learned From Teaching
paragraphs: I taught a Saturday reading class for one term, to eight children who were behind in reading.
I prepared carefully for the first lesson and it went badly. They could not read the passage I had chosen.
So I threw the plan away and asked them to bring something they wanted to read. One boy brought a football magazine.
We read the football magazine for three weeks. Then he asked for a book about footballers, and then a newspaper.
He is still not a strong reader. But he reads, and that is the difference I was actually there to make.
